conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS, to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. This is simply a routine way to see how mood, anxiety, and coping have been going for you in the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting, and there are no right or wrong answers. Everything you share stays confidential, and my goal is to create a comfortable, supportive space where you can speak freely. We’ll walk through ten short questions together—some about mood, others about how things like sleep or appetite have felt. Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Um… I guess sometimes I can still laugh—like if my husband makes a dumb joke while we’re changing diapers—but it feels kind of forced. Mostly I’m just tired, so even things that used to crack me up feel kind of “meh.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I mean, I can laugh, but it doesn’t come as easy as it used to. A couple of times this week my partner did something silly and I caught myself smiling, but it felt kind of flat—like I had to push myself to really enjoy it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to look forward to stuff—like my mom’s coming over tomorrow to see the baby—but honestly the excitement feels kind of dim. Even the idea of a quiet cup of coffee once he naps sounds nice, yet I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll just be tired again in an hour.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of nights ago he wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m just doing something wrong—like if I were better at this whole mom thing he’d sleep. It’s not constant, but little stuff like that makes me wonder if I’m messing him up already.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday he sneezed twice and my brain immediately jumped to “What if he’s getting really sick?” I knew it was probably nothing, but I kept checking his temperature and watching his breathing. It’s not all day, but those worries pop up out of nowhere and I can’t just shake them off right away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—I haven’t had that can’t-breathe, heart-racing thing—but every so often, when he’s napping, I’ll get this quick wave of “what if he just stops breathing?” It’s like a sudden flash of fear, then it fades. Doesn’t stick around long, but it sure catches me off-guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—he wouldn’t nap unless I held him, the laundry pile looked like a mountain, and I kept thinking, “How is everyone else doing this?” I managed to get through it, but I felt stretched thin and on edge the rest of the afternoon.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then lie there running through every little thing: Did I wash the bottles right? Is he warm enough? I probably drop off eventually, but it takes a while, and I wake up feeling like I never really rested.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—not every minute, but it sneaks in. Like the other afternoon I was feeding him and suddenly felt this heavy, gloomy wave. It passed after a bit, but those moments keep popping up a few times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when he wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch—but full-out crying hasn’t happened. Mostly I just feel tired and kind of flat, not weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’m worn out, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be okay for my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source of data: Patient self-report on 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire

Symptoms endorsed:  
- Diminished pleasure/joy (“flat” laughter, blunted excitement)  
- Intermittent low mood (“heavy, gloomy waves”)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant care  
- Intrusive, unrealistic worries about infant health/safety  
- Brief surges of fear re: SIDS while baby sleeps  
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks; “stretched thin”  
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminating about infant care  
- No tearfulness; denies self-harm ideation

Pattern: Sub-threshold depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety features; functioning intact but strained.

Screening significance:  
- Probable mild-to-moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety  
- No current safety concerns (denies suicidal/harmful thoughts)  
- Sleep disruption and guilt cognitions are potential exacerbators; early intervention may prevent escalation

Plan: Provide scoring sheet; discuss further evaluation (PHQ-9, GAD-7), psychoeducation, supportive counseling, and follow-up within 1–2 weeks.
